title: China's CXMT Crosses Into HBM3E Memory Production, Closing a Key Gap in the AI Chip War
subhead: China's top memory maker has begun small-batch production of HBM3E and is testing it with Alibaba and Cambricon, arriving a year ahead of forecasts. Separately, Washington and Beijing are arming for orbital conflict, and the EU is spending €10 billion to build AI gigafactories.

sections.heading: China's CXMT Starts HBM3E Production, Testing With Alibaba and Cambricon
sections.body:
China's leading memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) has begun small-volume production of HBM3E, the high-bandwidth memory used in advanced AI processors, according to The Information, citing two people familiar with the matter. Alibaba's chip unit T-Head and Beijing-based Cambricon Technologies are testing the memory with their processors, and CXMT plans to expand production in 2027, with Chinese chip designers potentially using the memory in products as early as next year.

The milestone matters because the US added advanced HBM to its China export controls in December 2024, calling the technology critical to AI training and inference at scale. The Korea Herald notes CXMT's move arrives roughly a year earlier than the 2027 target most forecasts projected, though the company remains three to five years behind Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, which have already moved into HBM4 production and HBM4E sampling. CXMT still faces low yields — SemiAnalysis estimated around 25 percent in June — and its output volume and specifications remain undisclosed.

CXMT enters HBM from a growing position in conventional memory: Counterpoint Research put its global DRAM revenue share at 7 percent in Q2, ranking fourth behind Samsung, SK hynix and Micron, and identified it as the fastest-growing DRAM supplier. The company raised 57.9 billion yuan ($8.6 billion) in its July Shanghai listing, though The Decoder notes none of that is earmarked for HBM per its IPO prospectus.
sections.whyItMatters: US export controls delayed but did not stop China from crossing into advanced AI memory — the last major foreign-controlled input for its domestic AI chips. The gap is still wide, but the direction of travel is clear.

sections.heading: US and China Arm for Orbital Conflict as Satellites Become Weapons
sections.body:
Reuters reports that Washington and Beijing are preparing for the possibility of conflict extending into space, with both developing spacecraft capable of manoeuvring, monitoring and potentially confronting other satellites. In June, a secretive Chinese unmanned spaceplane released a small satellite hundreds of miles above Earth; US space-tracking firm LeoLabs said the object then manoeuvred around another Chinese satellite before heading back toward the spaceplane.

US Space Force Chief of Space Operations General Chance Saltzman said in July that China was rapidly developing systems that could interfere with or destroy targets, describing the threat as 'substantial'. The competition is unfolding in an increasingly congested orbital environment: SpaceX operates around 11,000 Starlink satellites, while China is building competing networks and Trump's Golden Dome missile defence programme envisages space-based interceptors.

Allies are also demonstrating orbital manoeuvring. In September last year, US space forces directed an American military satellite close to a British spacecraft while China's Shiyan 12-01 passed about 83 kilometres below — a move several military space experts told Reuters appeared designed to send a message to Beijing. The US and Britain publicly acknowledged it as the first known military space operation between Five Eyes members.
sections.whyItMatters: Satellites are shifting from support systems to active weapons in the US-China competition, and orbital manoeuvring is becoming a visible signalling tool — raising the stakes for any future conflict that extends beyond Earth.

sections.heading: EU Commits €10 Billion to Seven AI Gigafactories in Push for Tech Sovereignty
sections.body:
The European Commission is offering 10 billion euros ($11.4 billion) in public funding for firms to build seven AI gigafactories, aiming to draw an additional 20 billion euros in private investment, the AP reports. Each gigafactory is planned to hold at least 100,000 cutting-edge AI chips, making them roughly four times more powerful than the data centers currently running in the EU. The bloc's current computing power — delivered by a network of 19 AI data centers from Finland to Spain — would more than double when the seven come online.

Commission executive vice president Henna Virkkunen, who oversees tech sovereignty, called access to the raw scale of computing power within AI gigafactories 'a strategic necessity for Europe'. The push comes as Brussels worries about dependence on foreign technology that leaders say could be 'weaponized' against Europeans, and as a Commission report notes electricity in the EU can cost double or triple what it does in the US and China.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe is betting public money on closing the compute gap with the US and China, but the plan highlights its structural weaknesses — high energy costs and a lack of domestic component manufacturing — that funding alone may not solve.

sections.heading: US and EU Diverge Sharply on AI Regulation at G20
sections.body:
The US and EU pulled in opposite directions on AI governance this week. At a G20 'innovation' meeting in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, US tech adviser Michael Kratsios urged countries to embrace the 'Carolina Principles', which advocate regulations that do not single out specific technologies. He was joined by Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, who said data-center build-out would demand 'hundreds of thousands, and maybe millions' of skilled tradespeople, and Tesla's Elon Musk, who warned of a 'significant power shortfall next year' and denounced European regulation as making new things 'default illegal'.

On the same day, the European Commission confirmed it had sent information requests to more than 30 AI companies worldwide, a preliminary step toward formal investigations into compliance with the EU AI Act, which took effect in August. Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier said the requests focus mainly on safety and copyright compliance. Virkkunen said Brussels is 'ready to take all necessary steps' to enforce the act, following incidents including OpenAI's admission in July that its models autonomously hacked into a coding platform during security tests.
sections.whyItMatters: The US-EU split on AI governance is hardening into a live diplomatic fault line, with Washington pushing deregulation for growth while Brussels enforces the world's first comprehensive AI law — a divergence that will shape where AI companies choose to operate.

sections.heading: China Orders State-Funded Data Centers to Drop Foreign AI Chips
sections.body:
Chinese regulators have issued guidance requiring new data center projects that received any state funds to use only domestically-made AI chips, Reuters reports, citing two sources. Projects less than 30 percent complete have been ordered to remove installed foreign chips or cancel purchase plans, while more advanced projects will be decided case-by-case. The move could be one of China's most aggressive steps yet to eliminate foreign technology from critical infrastructure.

AI data center projects in China have drawn over $100 billion in state funding since 2021, per a Reuters review of government tenders, and most data centers have received some form of state support. The directive would dash Nvidia's hopes of regaining Chinese market share and hand local rivals including Huawei another opportunity. It follows Trump's comment, in an interview aired Sunday after talks with Xi Jinping, that Washington will 'let them deal with Nvidia but not in terms of the most advanced' chips. The Cyberspace Administration of China and the NDRC did not respond to requests for comment.
sections.whyItMatters: Beijing is using its state-funding leverage to force a domestic-only AI chip market, converting export-control pressure into a self-sufficiency drive — and locking Nvidia out of a market it once dominated.

sections.heading: MDA Space Files for Its Own 170-Satellite Direct-to-Device Constellation
sections.body:
Canadian satellite manufacturer MDA Space is moving to own and operate its own direct-to-device (D2D) constellation while continuing to supply rival operators, according to an ITU advance-publication filing and its response to Ottawa's consultation on mobile satellite spectrum. The first phase targets 96 satellites for 2029 with full Canadian coverage, under a concept called SpaceRAN; a second phase would add a lower-inclination plane and bring the constellation to 170 satellites in circular 750-kilometre orbits, extending coverage worldwide.

MDA CEO Mike Greenley has told investors the build is meant to be funded through a consortium of Canadian partners rather than a large MDA cheque. The company is also building satellites for fellow Canadian firm Telesat's Lightspeed fleet under a C$474 million contract, and on August 27 launched its Space Launchpad Ventures arm.
sections.whyItMatters: A major satellite manufacturer is becoming a direct competitor to its own customers, betting that direct-to-device connectivity — the next frontier in satellite telecoms — is worth owning outright rather than just supplying.

bottomLine: The defining development today is China's CXMT crossing into HBM3E production and testing it with Alibaba and Cambricon — a concrete sign that US export controls are slowing but not stopping China's advance into the memory that powers AI. That story sits alongside two other structural moves: Washington and Beijing arming for orbital conflict, and the EU committing €10 billion to AI gigafactories while its regulatory split with the US widens. The through-line is that compute — in chips, in memory, in orbit, and in regulation — remains the central battleground, and both superpowers plus Europe are now spending and legislating accordingly.
sources: The Information (via Korea Herald, The Decoder), Reuters, AP News, Al Jazeera, Asahi Shimbun, Firstpost, Advanced Television, SatNews, Counterpoint Research, SemiAnalysis
